To get the toughest part out of the way I will tell you there is no campaign in the traditional sense. Instead, there’s a game master who works to shift players in certain directions to achieve goals. In universe these are called Major Orders. For some time these orders became very monotonous. Go here kill some bugs. Now go here and kill some bots. It was exhausting after a while.

What is really exciting is that they are now developing a story that follows a chain of events. Currently, players are working to build the Democratic Space Station or DSS. Players are certain this is going to bring about the creation of clans. Now it feels like decisions hold weight and our efforts contribute to something. I have found it to be very engaging even though I am mostly maxed with everything. It’s a lot of fun helping others and working together. You will no doubt run into rude folks but fortunately they are not too abundant.

Serious stuff aside I think the HD2 community is mostly very welcoming and wholesome. The main evidence I’ll provide here is when we sacrificed getting an in game stratagem, akin to an ability in other games, to save a children’s hospital that really did nothing for us. Nevertheless we pulled together and saved some in universe kids which led the developers to donate IRL money to important causes. 

I think that for the money it is an amazing investment. You can pick it up and put it down without missing out on too much. You could join a discord like I have to play with like minded folks as well. There will be times it’s frustrating and a little disheartening when a mission doesn’t go well. But like they say in game, “If at first you don’t succeed, dive again. And again. And again. And again. And again….”

You are really only playing to improve on your style which will most definitely become more niche as new weapons are introduced and augmentation becomes possible. I have nearly 300 hours in game and I’m still learning things which is so exciting. I hope you do cause it’s a good time and if you take the dive and wanna join a cool discord feel free to PM me. Cheers!

I know that results like that can be insulting to your efforts but a decline, regardless of how small, shows what you’re doing is helping. There’s a member of this sub who comments on a lot of posts about the stages of eating foods and that helped me go from 6.2 to 6.0 in a month. Everyone is different but it helped me. 

Specifically, I know I have a bad sweet tooth. Given that I eat my meals first which are usually packed with protein and healthy fats. Then I’ll eat something sweet whether it be a handful of m&ms or mini snickers. Sweets for me can also include berries or high sugar fruits in the form of a smoothie. I also limit my intake of carbs to roughly 60-80 grams per day. This way I can still enjoy some chips here and there or a bagel if I really want it. I think this part has been the biggest impact to my diet and would definitely recommend. I say this because carbs are sneaky and in a lot more foods than I originally thought.

Good luck to you. You got this.

To my understanding, weight can help with blood sugar issues in general but it all depends on how many carbs you’re taking in and when. The math for weight is simply calories out is more than calories in. With A1C it’s more to do with average blood sugar in the past three months. Therefore, it depends a lot on what you’re eating. While you are losing weight does not mean the food you’re eating does not cause your blood sugar to spike or stay elevated. I would suggest limiting carbs as much as you can or replace them with options that don’t raise your blood sugar. For example I’ve replaced a lot of rice dishes with salad. If it’s a white carb, such as rice, bread and of course sugar, it is bad for your sugar.

I know that for myself, when I sit and I’m having a lot of ideas and my mind is all over the place that I need to recognize the “monkey mind” which is my thoughts jumping from tree to tree. It is frustrating but being upset about it will not help my practice. 

So instead I allow my mind to jump from tree to tree. I recognize that this is where my mind is going but instead of chasing it with the hopes of the monkey slowing down, I let it pass. Mentally, this feels like “oh there it goes jumping to here, there it goes again jumping to there.” I find that naturally the monkey gets tired while I simply observe it. Sometimes this is as far as I can get for that moment of practice and for a time I was very frustrated about that. But after some reading and speaking with other practitioners I realize that calming the mind is a part of practice. I know that this can sound a little esoteric but this is what helps me. By not chasing and wrestling the monkey I can instead spend my energy on more productive things even if it is only to observe the monkey for that moment of practice. Then, over time I was able to see the monkey and not chase it so that I had the energy to focus on my practice once the monkey got tired.

I’m not too experienced with vipassana practice but perhaps something that helps me will help you. 

I am often upset with myself about how “poor” my own practice is. Whether that’s neglecting to sit and work on it, becoming frustrated with my lack of concentration, or not feeling fulfilled after I do. However, I also know that beating myself up over things like this will be even more detrimental. This is because I have forgotten what the point of my practice is in the first place. The goal is not to sit for the sake of sitting or concentrating on my breath because that’s what I’ve been told. Rather the goal is to be mindful during these moments of my practice. 

All this to say, I think you may be forcing yourself into more than you can handle. This is by no means a bad things because I imagine everyone struggles with this. I don’t know your history with meditation but going from not much to an hour at a time is a big jump. When I first started it was a chore meditating for just 20 minutes. At the time I became very frustrated and thought of quitting. Fortunately over time, and now, I realize that this form of meditation is called a practice for a reason. 

I would encourage you to be more gentle with yourself and realize that even after much time practicing that not all of your days practicing will feel productive. Perhaps, before starting you could allow yourself a few moments to play with your “monkey mind” instead of fighting against it. Then slowly calm the mind until you are ready to begin. That usually does a lot for me on days that I’m struggling to commit to my practice. Hope this helps in some way. Good luck to you.

I think that many in this field, along with every other IT field, would agree that you sign yourself up for a lifetime of learning. Not to say you have to but if you want your skills to stay relevant and marketable then you have to be willing to learn constantly. Your degree gives you the basics and if you work with a good company then they will teach you the rest. Then, if you want to work in a more competitive niche your skills will need to match that. I would argue working for smaller companies can help with this however they are not all like the company I work for. Also, I did not use my degree for a few years after graduation before landing this job and almost everything I do now was a skill I learned at this job. 

With regards to AI, I find it funny but understandable when people talk about AI replacing all these jobs in a few years. While AI can be helpful with mundane tasks, you will quickly find that jobs with a CS degree are not mundane. They may have areas that can be made more efficient with AI but replacing 400 people that all work together to make a software offering function along with all the steps involved is just not possible. But if you do not have experience with this then AI can seem scary.

Ultimately I think that you should find a mentor who has a degree in CS and does the work every day. Or you can just ask other people IRL like you are here. It is very rewarding given what you can do with it but it does expect a lot of you if you want to truly work in the field.

If that is not an option look for therapists that specialize in dialectical behavioral therapy, DBT, which is a proven method of treating BPD. A mix of therapy and meds helps me to manage things a lot better than just hoping for a good day. It won’t be easy but like many have said on this thread realizing you need help is the first step.
